questions.q: Why did the Edsel's 'The Edsel is Coming' teaser campaign ultimately work against the car?
options: It revealed too many technical details, so buyers lost interest before launch
It built months of secrecy and anticipation that the actual car could not possibly live up to on E-Day
It was so expensive that there was no money left to build the cars
It targeted the wrong country and never reached American buyers
questions.explanation: By hiding the car and showing only a shadow or the hood ornament, Ford drove public curiosity to an enormous pitch. When the curtain finally lifted on E-Day, the strange, divisive styling could not match months of breathless mystery, so the hype became a trap.

questions.q: Why do designers conduct market research prior to designing a new product?
options: To develop a possible marketing campaign
To determine the level of consumer demand
To access alternative manufacturing techniques
To understand the impact of a life cycle analysis
questions.explanation: Market research carried out before designing identifies consumer needs and gauges the level of demand, confirming there is a market for the product. A marketing campaign is developed later to sell the product, not the reason research is done up front.

questions.q: What was the fatal flaw buried inside Ford's seemingly airtight market research for the Edsel?
options: The sample of consumers surveyed was far too small to be reliable
It described the medium-priced market of the early 1950s, not the world the car was actually launched into — a recession and a shift to small, compact cars
It focused only on engineering data and ignored consumer opinion entirely
It was never actually completed before the car went on sale
questions.explanation: The research was thorough but read the wrong future: it nailed the needs of a market that had already moved on. By 1957 the boom was in compact cars and the US had slid into recession, so Ford launched expensive medium-priced models exactly when buyers wanted cheaper and smaller.

questions.q: Which combination of factors most influences the success of an innovation?
options: Social demand and cultural values
Product demand and social implications
Timing and appropriate marketing strategies
Ease of use and economical manufacturing processes
questions.explanation: The success of an innovation depends largely on timing — releasing the product when the market is ready — combined with appropriate marketing strategies to reach consumers. Even a strong product can fail if it is mistimed or poorly marketed.

questions.q: Why did quality control on the Edsel fall apart despite its clever features like the rolling-dome speedometer and Teletouch transmission?
options: The features were too advanced to manufacture with 1950s technology
Ford launched the Edsel as a brand-new division without its own factory, so resentful Ford workers assembled it on regular Ford lines and took little pride in it
The recession forced Ford to use cheaper materials than planned
Dealers refused to stock spare parts for the new models
questions.explanation: The fatal management decision was launching a new division with no dedicated factory. Edsels were built by Ford workers who resented building 'someone else's car', so quality collapsed — cars arrived with notes listing missing parts, and the untrained Teletouch transmission became the biggest mechanical headache.

questions.q: Which of the following is most important for an innovative idea to be successful?
options: A comprehensive marketing plan
Workload management and state of the art equipment
Thorough planning, research, timing and consumer demand
Using local and current technologies for immediate release in the marketplace
questions.explanation: Successful innovation depends on thorough planning and research, good timing and genuine consumer demand — without a real market need even a well-marketed idea fails. A marketing plan alone cannot make a product succeed if these underlying factors are not met.

questions.q: From memory, list the stack of factors that together killed the Edsel. (There is more than one.)
keyPoints: Market research was thorough but read the wrong future — it served a market that had already moved on.
Timing collided with a recession and a shift to small, compact cars.
Branding threw away the trusted Ford name and saddled the car with a clumsy name (Edsel Ford), giving it no existing customer base.
The aesthetics/styling were strange and divisive.
Quality and manufacturing were a mess because the new division was never given its own properly set-up factory.
questions.explanation: The point of the case study is that it wasn't one mistake but a stack of them. If you recalled at least the research/timing failure, the branding problem and the manufacturing/quality failure, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: In your own words, what is the central design lesson the Edsel teaches about product versus market focus?
keyPoints: A design can be expensively researched, cleverly engineered and brilliantly marketed and still fail completely.
It fails if it answers a need that has already gone, arrives at the wrong moment, and isn't built well.
When designing the Edsel, Ford was focused on the product and not nearly interested enough in the market.
questions.explanation: The Edsel is in the course because it bundles every success/failure factor into one story. The crux is that doing everything 'by the book' on the product side cannot rescue a design that ignores the market and its timing.

questions.q: Outline ONE factor that could affect the success or failure of a design.
questions.modelAnswer: One important factor is functionality — how well a product, system or environment performs its intended purpose. If the design fails to perform its intended function efficiently, it may result in design failure. (Other valid factors include the appropriateness of the design solution, needs, aesthetics, finance/cost, ergonomics, obsolescence and time.)

criteria.descriptor: Outlines a factor that could affect the impact on the success or failure of a design

questions.explanation: Using the Edsel, a strong answer could outline timing, market research, branding or quality of manufacture as the chosen factor — each one demonstrably affected whether the car succeeded or failed.

questions.q: Analyse how economic, historical and timing factors determine the success or failure of designs.
questions.modelAnswer: Economic, historical and timing factors all strongly determine whether a design succeeds or fails. Economically, a product released during a negative climate of high interest rates and low disposable income is less likely to be embraced, so designers must time release to a positive climate or to when the product is most needed — for example launching a Dyson air fan in the warmer spring and summer season, when consumers prioritise cooling even in tough economic times, rather than in winter at a high price. Governments may also provide incentives, financial support and favourable trade conditions in poor periods, improving the economic viability of design and production. Yet some designs succeed regardless of high purchase and upgrade costs: Apple phones and music devices dominate the market because effective marketing makes them perceived as needed and essential, showing that perceived need and timing of release can outweigh pure economic viability. Together these economic, historical and timing factors determine not only sales to the target market but also the broader acceptance and desirability of a design in society.

criteria.descriptor: Draws out and relates implications of how economic, historical and timing factors affect the success or failure of designs
Provides reasons through the use of cause and effect as to how economic, historical and timing factors affect the success or failure of designs
Identifies issues and provides evidence of how economic, historical and timing factors affect the success or failure of designs
Provides characteristics and features of how at least TWO of these factors (economic, historical and timing) affect the success or failure of designs
Sketches in general terms how economic and/or historical and/or timing factors affect the success and/or failure of designs
Identifies a feature of economic or historical or timing factors that affects the success and/or failure of designs

questions.explanation: The Edsel is a textbook illustration: it launched into a recession (economic), at the moment the market had shifted from medium-priced to compact cars (historical), and three years too late for the world its research described (timing) — so all three factors combined to doom an otherwise well-funded design.
